items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the boundary between weathered material (regolith) and unweathered bedrock”.

items.markingKey: Weathering front: the boundary between weathered material (regolith) and unweathered bedrock. [1]

items.stem: Explain why weathering profiles are so deep in the humid tropics.
items.answer: High temperatures speed chemical reactions; abundant rainfall all year provides water; organic acids from rapid decay; long periods of stability without glaciation or erosion; joints allow water to penetrate deeply.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Describe a typical deep weathering profile in granite.
items.answer: From the surface down: soil and lateritic crust; completely weathered clay-rich saprolite; partially weathered zone with corestones; weathering front; fresh jointed bedrock.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per zone in order [4]

items.stem: “Climate is the most important factor in explaining the depth of weathering in tropical environments.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to relief and rock type.
items.answer: For: High temperatures and rainfall drive rapid chemical weathering (hydrolysis, carbonation, chelation). Against: Rock type and jointing, time and tectonic stability (Gondwana shields), relief and drainage, vegetation and erosion rates control how deep profiles become. Conclusion: Climate sets the rate, but depth depends on long periods of stability, rock structure and slow removal of regolith.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “weathering front”?
options: The layer of loose, weathered material lying above solid bedrock.
Chemically weathered rock that has rotted in place but keeps its original structure.
A rounded block of less-weathered rock surrounded by saprolite in a weathering profile.
The boundary between weathered material (regolith) and unweathered bedrock.
items.answer: The boundary between weathered material (regolith) and unweathered bedrock.

items.stem: Explain how the weathering front can later be exposed to form landforms.
items.answer: Changes in base level or climate increase erosion, which strips away the regolith (etching), exposing corestones and the irregular weathering front as tors and inselbergs.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an isolated, steep-sided hill rising abruptly from a plain, typical of tropical shield areas”.

items.stem: Explain the formation of inselbergs.
items.answer: Deep chemical weathering penetrates further where joints are closely spaced; areas of massive rock remain unweathered; later stripping of regolith (base-level fall, climate change) exposes these as isolated hills; scarp retreat and pediplanation (King) may also contribute.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: Explain the role of jointing in the formation of granite landforms.
items.answer: Joint spacing controls where water penetrates and chemical weathering is concentrated; widely jointed rock forms domes (bornhardts); closely jointed rock breaks into blocks (tors, kopjes); sheet joints shape domes.

items.answer: (a) Generally, hills with more widely spaced joints stand higher. (b) Too small for statistical testing (e.g. Spearman’s rank needs about 8-10); other factors such as rock composition may vary.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the formation of granite landforms in the tropics is explained better by deep weathering than by slope retreat.
items.answer: For: Exposed weathering fronts, corestones and etchplains support the two-stage theory (Thomas, Linton); joints control where weathering penetrates. Against: King’s parallel slope retreat and pediplanation explain inselbergs in semi-arid Africa; multiple cycles of weathering and stripping and climate change complicate both. Conclusion: Deep weathering explains many tropical granite landforms, but slope retreat and climate change are needed to explain their exposure and shape.

items.stem: Compare the theories of King and Thomas for the origin of inselbergs.
items.answer: King: parallel retreat of slopes in semi-arid conditions leaves residual hills above pediplains. Thomas: deep weathering beneath a humid climate followed by stripping (two-stage).

items.stem: Explain the formation of cockpit karst.
items.answer: Solution is concentrated where water drains into depressions along joints; depressions deepen and enlarge into star-shaped cockpits; the intervening areas remain as conical hills; heavy rainfall and organic acids speed the process.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [3]

items.stem: Explain the formation of tower karst.
items.answer: Solution of limestone down to a level of the water table or impermeable rock leaves isolated towers; lateral solution by swamps and rivers at the base (foot caves) undercuts and steepens them; alluvial plains form between towers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the landforms of tropical karst are mainly the result of climate. In your answer you may refer to solution and base level.
items.answer: For: Intense rainfall and biogenic CO₂ produce rapid solution and large cockpits and towers (Guilin, Jamaica, Ha Long Bay). Against: Rock purity, jointing, uplift and base level, tectonic history and allogenic rivers control where towers and cockpits develop; similar forms occur in some non-tropical areas. Conclusion: Climate accounts for the intensity and scale of tropical karst, but geology and tectonics determine its form and distribution.

items.stem: A student writes: “Cold water dissolves limestone faster, so tropical karst should be less developed.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Although cold water holds more CO₂, tropical soils produce far more CO₂ and rainfall is greater, so tropical solution rates are high.

items.stem: Explain why tropical karst differs from temperate karst.
items.answer: Higher rainfall, temperatures and biogenic CO₂ cause more rapid solution, producing larger-scale positive landforms (towers, cones) rather than mainly negative forms (pavements, dolines).

items.stem: What is meant by the term “tower karst”?
options: A landscape of closely spaced conical hills separated by star-shaped depressions (cockpits), as in Jamaica.
A landscape of steep-sided, isolated limestone hills (towers) rising from a flat plain, such as around Guilin, China.
A closed depression in limestone formed by solution or collapse.
The reaction between carbonic acid and calcium carbonate, producing soluble calcium bicarbonate.
items.answer: A landscape of steep-sided, isolated limestone hills (towers) rising from a flat plain, such as around Guilin, China.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Karst towers are always surrounded by flat alluvial plains.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Some form in groups on uplifted plateaus or are drowned by the sea (Ha Long Bay).
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Cold water dissolves limestone faster, so tropical karst should be less developed.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the formation of tower karst.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Although cold water holds more CO₂, tropical soils produce far more CO₂ and rainfall is greater, so tropical solution rates are high. (b) Solution of limestone down to a level of the water table or impermeable rock leaves isolated towers; lateral solution by swamps and rivers at the base (foot caves) undercuts and steepens them; alluvial plains form between towers.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: “The landforms of tropical karst are mainly the result of climate.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to rock structure and uplift.
items.answer: For: Intense rainfall and biogenic CO₂ produce rapid solution and large cockpits and towers (Guilin, Jamaica, Ha Long Bay). Against: Rock purity, jointing, uplift and base level, tectonic history and allogenic rivers control where towers and cockpits develop; similar forms occur in some non-tropical areas. Conclusion: Climate accounts for the intensity and scale of tropical karst, but geology and tectonics determine its form and distribution.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the weathering front can later be exposed to form landforms. (b) Describe a typical deep weathering profile in granite.
items.answer: (a) Changes in base level or climate increase erosion, which strips away the regolith (etching), exposing corestones and the irregular weathering front as tors and inselbergs. (b) From the surface down: soil and lateritic crust; completely weathered clay-rich saprolite; partially weathered zone with corestones; weathering front; fresh jointed bedrock.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark per zone in order [4]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why weathering profiles are so deep in the humid tropics. (b) Explain how the weathering front can later be exposed to form landforms.
items.answer: (a) High temperatures speed chemical reactions; abundant rainfall all year provides water; organic acids from rapid decay; long periods of stability without glaciation or erosion; joints allow water to penetrate deeply. (b) Changes in base level or climate increase erosion, which strips away the regolith (etching), exposing corestones and the irregular weathering front as tors and inselbergs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per factor [4] (b) [3]

items.stem: “Climate is the most important factor in explaining the depth of weathering in tropical environments.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to vegetation and relief.
items.answer: For: High temperatures and rainfall drive rapid chemical weathering (hydrolysis, carbonation, chelation). Against: Rock type and jointing, time and tectonic stability (Gondwana shields), relief and drainage, vegetation and erosion rates control how deep profiles become. Conclusion: Climate sets the rate, but depth depends on long periods of stability, rock structure and slow removal of regolith.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Tors can form by deep weathering and stripping.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Inselbergs only form in present-day hot deserts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Linton’s two-stage theory explains Dartmoor tors this way. (b) Not correct. Many formed under humid tropical weathering and are now found in savanna and arid lands.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Compare the theories of King and Thomas for the origin of inselbergs. (b) A student writes: “Inselbergs only form in present-day hot deserts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) King: parallel retreat of slopes in semi-arid conditions leaves residual hills above pediplains. Thomas: deep weathering beneath a humid climate followed by stripping (two-stage). (b) Not correct. Many formed under humid tropical weathering and are now found in savanna and arid lands.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Rock structure and jointing influence the pattern of cockpits.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why tropical karst differs from temperate karst.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Solution follows joints, so depressions are aligned with them. (b) Higher rainfall, temperatures and biogenic CO₂ cause more rapid solution, producing larger-scale positive landforms (towers, cones) rather than mainly negative forms (pavements, dolines).
